paragraphs.text: Traditional grammar divided sentences into a small number of different types according to their structures (forms) for instance, indicative, imperative and interrogative. While this is of some use for certain purposes, such a classification is quite inadequate for revealing the great variety of functions which sentences can be used to perform. A sentence which is structurally interrogative, such as 'Would you pass the salt?', might be used to ask a question, make a request or issue a command, for example. An indicative sentence is probably even more versatile it may be used to warn, state, hypothesise, describe, report, promise, etc. A proper understanding of the functions of sentences would have to go well beyond traditional structural classifications.

Many philosophers studying language have focused upon a very narrow sector of language upon sentences which are basically being used to state facts. However, this can lead to an obsession with assessing sentences only as being true or false. Such a focus ignores the many other interesting ways in which what people say can be assessed. For example, in the case of moral and aesthetic judgments like 'This is good' or 'This is beautiful', it could be argued that they are neither true nor false. They can still be assessed, however, but in different ways from sentences, which can be demonstrated to be true or false, such as scientific hypotheses. Again, the laws of the land cannot be said to be true or false, since they are best considered as rules or commands. Yet obviously one wants to be able to assess laws, and this can be done in terms other than true or false.

J. L. Austin was the first philosopher to focus not on the word or the sentence, but on the act which a person performs with the aid of words or sentences: the theory of language becoming, as it were, a branch of the theory of action. Just as some acts performed in a game of football have a specific meaning -as when kicking a ball into a net counts as scoring -so there are 'speech acts', such as stating, reporting, questioning, and so on.

Austin's programme was roughly this: first, to present the variety of acts which can be performed with language, and in particular to distinguish many of these from the acts of stating reporting, or describing. Second, to lay down a framework for describing the ways in which speech acts can go right or wrong. Finally, to reveal the different aspects of speech acts, as a speech act consists of a complex system of sub-acts, rather than being a single, indivisible act.

Austin's initial distinction among speech acts is between 'constative' and 'performative' utterances. A constative utterance, roughly, serves to state a fact, report that something is the case or describe what something is Performative utterances, on the other hand, do not describe or report or state, they are not ‘true’ or ‘false’; and the uttering of the sentence is, or is part of, the doing of an action.

Examples of performative utterances will help here. Take the sentences ‘I promise to come to dinner’ and ‘I hereby appoint you Prime Minister’. Neither of these describes anything. ‘I promise.. ‘does not describe an act of promising (unlike say, ‘I promised to come to dinner); rather in context, the uttering of these words is the act of making a promise. ‘I hereby appoint you...‘ does not report an appointment; in context, it is the making of an appointment. Not being descriptions of anything, promises and appointments are neither true nor false. A promise can be sincere or insincere, wise or stupid, but not true or false. To suppose that ‘I promise...’ is a true or false description may lead us into philosophical error. If it were a description, and therefore true or false we would probably expect it to describe an inner, mental act of promising. But we do not know what inner, mental acts are going on inside other people, so how could we ever know whether people were really making promises or not? Yet, of course, we do often know that people make promises, if they utter the right words in the right context. What they are actually thinking doesn't come into it Performative utterances do not have to be explicit. To make a promise I need not say 'I promise...’; it may be enough, given certain circumstances, for me to say ‘I will.... Again, I can appoint someone to a position without using the explicit formula 'I hereby appoint...’

Performatives are neither true nor fail if it is made insincerely, for example, if I say ‘I promise...’ but do not intend to keep to my word. In this case, although I can be said to have promised, the promise has partially failed: it is not a straightforward, fully effective promise. There is a difference between this promise and one which I fully intend to keep.

questions.prompt: What claim is made about traditional grammar in the first paragraph?

options.text: It does not classify sentences into enough different structures.
It is useful for showing structural similarities between languages.
It cannot provide enough information about how language is used.
It can show the relationship between particular forms and particular functions.

questions.prompt: In the second paragraph, the writer refers to scientific hypotheses as

options.text: a form of language that is similar to laws.
examples of sentences that are true or false.
sentences that need further philosophical analysis.
an aspect of language that is generally ignored by philosophers.

questions.prompt: Football is mentioned in order to illustrate the claim that

options.text: the functions of language and of sport are quite different.
language can be used to carry out certain actions.
the analysis of language can illuminate the rules of sport.
words and sentences should be analysed before speech acts.

questions.prompt: According to the writer, part of Austin's aim was

options.text: to analys how speech acts can succeed or fail.
to identify the single element that each speech act consists of.
to demonstrate the relevance of speech acts to philosophy.
to produce a simplified analysis of language.

questions.prompt: What would have to be the case for a promise to be classified as a description?

options.text: The promise would have to be carried out.
The words used to make promises would have to be changed.
The promise would have to be confirmed by the speaker.
The speaker's thoughts would have to be known.

questions.prompt: According to the last paragraph, one reason for the complete failure of a performative utterance is that the speaker

options.text: fails to understand the significance of what he or she is saying.
is not authorised to carry out that particular act.
is addressing an inappropriate listener.
does not intend to carry out that act.
